text: Walking for Life

runs.text: Walking for Life

text: Regardless of age, size, fitness or health, walking is the entry-level physical activity with the most health benefits and the fewest risks. According to a 2015 study, a daily walk can            decrease blood pressure, resting heart and lower cholesterol in a person’s body. Walking can even improve cognitive function and boost a low mood. It requires no special clothing or footwear, or expensive equipment. Just put one foot in front of the other and get going. It is as easy as that.

text: There is no right or wrong way to walk. ‘We’re all designed biomechanically to walk in our         own individual way,’ says Dr Jim Stinear of the University of Auckland’s Department of           Exercise Sciences. ‘It’s partly genetic and can also be influenced by childhood habit or past injury. But essentially we’re creatures of our shape, bone length, muscle bulk and muscle attachment positions.’

text: Still, when it comes to getting fit, our bodies are working against us. ‘We’ve evolved to move        in a way that keeps the metabolic cost to a minimum,’ says Stinear, ‘presumably because we were designed to walk long distances.’ His advice is to increase the rhythm rather than try to change the stride. The guidelines for physical fitness are pretty clear. According to Stinear,         you need 150 minutes of accumulated walking a week at a brisk pace or in rolling           countryside, enough to cause the heart and breathing rates to increase. Just strolling round           the shops and your local area is not sufficient. Part of Stinear’s work involves helping to rehabilitate people who have suffered cancer, stroke and heart disease. ‘We never say don’t exercise, that’s for sure. Even if all people can manage is to get up off their chairs… we          advise them to do it regularly. The body hates to be inactive.’

text: Joining a walking group is one of the best and easiest ways to boost overall health, with             virtually no side effects, according to a 2015 report published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine. Researchers evaluated 42 studies, involving 2,000 patients in 14 countries who         had long-term illnesses including arthritis, dementia, diabetes, and Parkinson’s disease.         Those who joined walking groups registered increased lung power and their overall physical fitness also improved.

text: The benefits for older adults have been well documented. A recent Tufts University study of  men and women aged over 75 found that even modest physical activity, such as gardening,         was associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular disease. Picking up your walking pace and covering longer distances lowered the risk significantly. Earlier research on walking from the University of Georgia found that older adults can improve their health and increase their likelihood of maintaining independence and needing less help from others by 41% by taking          part in an exercise programme that involves walking for 40 continuous minutes, three times         a week. There is less scientific evidence when it comes to research on children, however pediatricians agree on the importance of encouraging them to be active from an early age.             ‘The patterns of behaviour we’re exposed to as a child affect how we behave as adults,’ says David Newman, president of the Paediatric Society. ‘Children of sedentary adults are likely to be sedentary themselves… that’s why we try to get kids used to regular exercise in pre-school.’

text: Other forms of exercise can strain small bodies, and there are concerns that excessive exercise – long-distance running or highly competitive sport – may leave still-growing kids vulnerable to repetitive stress injuries. But walking is friendly to young bones and joints. It’s just as helpful for aching old ones. A study from Tel Aviv University found it is as effective a therapy for alleviating pain located in the back as strengthening exercises that often require specific equipment and expert supervision.

text: So, how can you make walking a habit? The popularity of pedometers and similar electronic devices means many people recognise the benefits of reaching 10,000 steps a day. But the pace and effort of this is just as important as the number. Researchers at Ohio State University found that walking faster can burn 20% more calories than maintaining a steady pace.

text: Still, you don’t have to undertake anything too strenuous for a worthwhile boost to your health. Even moving from a neighbourhood that requires a vehicle to get around to one where walking is convenient has benefits, according to a recent study from the American Heart Association. Researchers found that people who moved to walking-friendly areas had a 54% lower risk of high blood pressure.

text: If you’re aiming to tackle something more demanding like a competition, you’ll want to take things more seriously. Auckland trainer Michael McCormack always emphasises the importance of the right kind of training to all his clients. ‘If you’re not properly conditioned,’ he explains, ‘you are going to struggle very early on.’

text: It sounds like hard work but the ultimate rewards might not only improve physical health but also enhance a person’s levels of happiness. A good example of this is Cheryl Strayed, author of the book Wild, who wrote of her solo hike along the Pacific Crest Trail which transformed her life in so many ways.
